modules.name: John H. Patterson
modules.outcome: Describe selling as a trained process, and judge when structure helps and when it turns into pressure, using the NCR Primer's own lines.
modules.intro: John H. Patterson gave National Cash Register salesmen a script, the Primer, that told them what to say and what to do while saying it. Its own lines show the two sides: honest advice about sympathy and sincerity, and closing tricks that a buyer could fairly call pressure.

blocks.x: The record behind this lesson

We read the Harvard Business School excerpt of Friedman's Business History Review article in full. It quotes the Primer directly. We read the rest of the article in an earlier pass, but its page now returns only a stub, so claims taken from it are marked and were not re-checked. {{friedman-hbs}} {{friedman-full}}
His method, step by step

i: Do not credit him with the invention. Scripts were rare but not new: Henry B. Hyde's Hints for Agents (1859), booklets for Bible Society canvassers, and Bates Harrington's How 'Tis Done (1879) came before the first NCR Primer in 1887. {{friedman-hbs}}

See what the script covered. The first sales script, How I Sell National Cash Registers, was written by Patterson's brother-in-law Joseph Crane and told salesmen what to do while speaking, with an asterisk meaning point to the item. {{friedman-hbs}}

Follow the four steps. Approach (no mention of the register; offer to help the merchant raise profit), proposition (first description of the register and how it prevents theft and gives an accurate daily account), demonstration (at a hotel display or the branch office), and close. {{friedman-hbs}}

Read the closing advice. It said not to ask for an order but to take it for granted, asking 'what colour shall I make it?' or 'how soon do you want delivery?', then fill in the order blank and hand over the pen. {{friedman-hbs}}

Read the warnings in the same text. 'Avoid giving the impression to the merchant that you are trying to force him to buy,' because 'no man likes to feel he is being sold,' and the first rules were sympathy for the buyer's business and sincerity. {{friedman-hbs}}

See that the script was revised. A Book of Arguments followed, then a Sales Manual in 1894 that combined the two, nearly two hundred pages by 1904, cut to a 56-page booklet by 1910 to make it easier to master. {{friedman-hbs}}

blocks.x: Friedman reports an agent's own account of selling: he says he sells a stranger the register that fits his needs, tells a buyer who thinks the price high that he does not blame him, and sometimes says he does not want to sell a register to someone who will not use it, because one misplaced register might spoil the sale of a dozen. Another agent sells the model the buyer asks for first and educates him afterwards, even if it is not the best fit. That is a limit, not a model. {{friedman-hbs}}

A former salesman, T. C. Henry, wrote in his 1913 book Tricks of the Cash Register Trust that every argument a merchant could raise had been thrashed out in the company's schools, and he called the company a shark. {{friedman-full}}

These sources describe a company of the 1880s to 1920s selling cash registers. The seven steps in this module come from a modern textbook, so the link to Patterson is the idea of a repeatable process, not the same steps. {{friedman-hbs}}

Can you show each benefit? Say what it cannot do.

Does the buyer get to try and question it?

For each step, write one thing you will say or do, and one thing you will not do. The Primer warned against forcing the sale. {{friedman-hbs}}

steps: The Sales Manual reached nearly 200 pages in 1904 and 56 pages in 1910. {{friedman-hbs}}
That is 56 ÷ 200 = 28% of the size, a cut of about 72%.

For your own page: if you cannot say each step from memory after three practices, shorten it.

o: Avoid giving the impression you are forcing the buyer
blocks.w: It warned that no man likes to feel he is being sold. {{friedman-hbs}}

modules.name: John H. Patterson
modules.outcome: Set a territory, a daily record and an honest target for prospecting, and note the limits of Patterson's methods.
modules.intro: Patterson's company divided the map into territories, recorded every call and set quotas, and used contests and conventions to drive effort. Those habits underpin prospecting and records. His pressure on rivals is the part to leave out.

blocks.x: The record behind this lesson

The Harvard Business School excerpt of Friedman's article states the management system in general terms. {{friedman-hbs}} The details on territories, daily reports, the sales school and quotas come from the full article and from Britannica, which we read in an earlier pass; the full article's page now returns only a stub, so those details were not re-checked. {{friedman-full}} {{brit-patterson}}
His method, step by step

i: Give each person a territory. Patterson assigned each salesman an exclusive territory. {{brit-patterson}}
Train before you send. He opened a sales school in 1894, with an initial course of six weeks. {{friedman-full}}
Record every call. Salesmen wrote daily reports listing the customers called on, the sales made and the prospects visited. {{friedman-full}}

Set a quota from a stated basis. Quotas were first set by the population of the territory, on his calculation that one register could be sold for every four hundred people, and later by the previous year's sales. {{friedman-full}}

Meet and compare. He held conventions and thematic sales contests, and the excerpt describes a system covering everything from quota calculation and commission rates to motivating discouraged salesmen. {{friedman-hbs}}

Leave out the hostility. The excerpt says he pressured salesmen to rid their regions of competition, and the reports also tracked competitors the company aimed to knock out. Aggressive tactics against rivals are not a model here. {{friedman-hbs}} {{friedman-full}}

blocks.x: The quota basis was crude, one register per 400 people, and it was replaced by past sales as experience grew. A target should come from your own record and move when the record does. {{friedman-full}}

blocks.title: Patterson's system and a personal version (the right column is our adaptation)
head: Element
In Patterson's company
Personal version
rows: An exclusive area for each salesman
A defined type of customer and area
Practise your process aloud before you go out
A daily report of calls, sales and prospects
Population first, then last year's sales
A target set from your own last month
Review weekly with a peer, not against them
blocks.src: The first two columns follow the sources. The last column is our adaptation. {{brit-patterson}} {{friedman-full}} {{friedman-hbs}}

blocks.x: Worked example: a quota from population (his rule, our arithmetic)

blocks.title: One register per 400 people
steps: A territory of 12,000 people at one register per 400 gives 12,000 ÷ 400 = 30 registers. {{friedman-full}}
A territory of 50,000 gives 50,000 ÷ 400 = 125.
If last year's sales in the first territory were 24, the later method would set this year's quota near 24, which is 80% of the population figure.
The population rule ignores the competition, price and local trade, which is why experience replaced it. {{friedman-full}}

blocks.x: Worked example: a prospecting week (illustrative numbers)

blocks.title: Territory, record, target
steps: Define your territory: a type of customer and an area. A clear boundary stops you drifting.
Set a target you can check, for example 20 qualified conversations in the week.
Keep a daily record: who you contacted, what happened and the next step. {{friedman-full}}
At the end of the week, count. If you had 12 conversations against a target of 20, you reached 60 per cent.
Adjust the target using last week's result, as Patterson's quotas moved to past volume. {{friedman-full}}

blocks.x: Apply it: your prospecting system

i: Define your territory in one sentence.
Set a weekly target from your own record.
Make a one-line daily log template.
Count at the end of the week and work out the percentage.
Adjust the target and write down why.

blocks.x: Define your territory, set a weekly target, and make a one-line daily record template.

blocks.q: How were NCR quotas first set?
o: By the population of the territory
blocks.w: Initially quotas were set according to the population of the territory. {{friedman-full}}

blocks.q: A territory of 12,000 people at one register per 400 gives what quota?
12 conversations against a target of 20 is what percentage?
blocks.w: 12 divided by 20 is 0.6, or 60 per cent.

i: Territory, record and target give prospecting a shape. {{friedman-full}}
Review results and adjust the target.
Avoid hostile tactics against rivals. {{friedman-hbs}}

quiz.q: What did NCR salesmen record in daily reports?
o: Customers called on, sales and prospects
quiz.w: Daily reports listed customers called on, sales made and prospects. {{friedman-full}}

modules.name: Dale Carnegie
modules.outcome: Use Carnegie's six ways to make people like you in your first thirty seconds, keep the interest genuine, and say what the critics said.
modules.intro: Dale Carnegie's How to Win Friends and Influence People gave short rules for dealing with people. The book is still in copyright and we did not read it, so this lesson works from the wording of its principles and from the reception, including the charge that the method can be insincere.

blocks.x: The record behind this lesson

We did not read the book. The principles below are quoted as worded in the Wikipedia article's lists, and the reception comes from the same article. Britannica's note on genuine interest comes from an earlier pass. {{carnegie-wiki}} {{brit-carnegie-book}}
His method, step by step

i: Know the book's shape. It was published by Simon & Schuster in late 1936, and the 1981 edition cut its sections from six to four. Carnegie called it an action-book. {{carnegie-wiki}}
Start with the fundamentals. The first part says: don't criticise, condemn or complain; give honest and sincere appreciation; arouse in the other person an eager want. {{carnegie-wiki}}

Learn the six ways. Become genuinely interested in other people; smile; remember a person's name is the sweetest and most important sound in any language; be a good listener and encourage others to talk about themselves; talk in terms of the other person's interest; make the other person feel important, and do it sincerely. {{carnegie-wiki}}

Notice the qualifiers. 'Genuinely' and 'sincerely' are in the wording of the principles. Britannica notes the emphasis on genuine interest rather than flattery. {{carnegie-wiki}} {{brit-carnegie-book}}

Know the criticism. Sinclair Lewis said the book taught people to smile and bob and pretend to be interested in other people's hobbies, and later scholars called Carnegie insincere and manipulative. {{carnegie-wiki}}
See the balanced early review. The New York Times in February 1937 said Carnegie offered insightful advice but that his wisdom was very simple and should not replace real knowledge. {{carnegie-wiki}}

blocks.x: These can be used as tricks. If the interest is not real, the buyer will often notice, and this module's lessons on fair selling apply. Use the list as habits of attention, not as a script. {{carnegie-wiki}}

Source
Sincerity check
rows: Become genuinely interested in other people
Can you name one thing you actually want to know about them?
Smile because you are glad to meet them, not to look keen
Write it down; use it to respect, not to manipulate
Talk in terms of their interest
Is what you say true of their situation?
Praise only what you actually noticed

That is 6 ÷ 10 = 60%. Set a target such as 8 of 10, and try repeating the name in conversation and writing it at once.

blocks.w: He criticised it as teaching people to smile and bob and pretend to be interested. {{carnegie-wiki}}

blocks.w: Britannica notes the emphasis on genuine interest. {{brit-carnegie-book}}

modules.name: Harry Gordon Selfridge
modules.outcome: Stage a presentation so the customer can see, handle and picture the product, thinking from the customer's side, without exaggeration.
modules.intro: Harry Gordon Selfridge wrote a book arguing that dependable statements pay and that a sales manager must think from the customer's standpoint. He treated windows and displays as a craft and the first contact with staff as the start of the customer's goodwill.

blocks.x: The record behind this lesson

We read chapter I of his 1918 book The Romance of Commerce, on honesty and advertising, and chapter XXIV, on the managers of a department store. It is his own book, so the claims about his methods are his. {{selfridge-roc}} The facts about the store come from Wikipedia. {{selfridge}} {{selfridges}}
His method, step by step

i: Begin from the customer's standpoint. The manager of sales must put himself in the place of the public and think from the standpoint of the customer. {{selfridge-roc}}
Treat the display as a craft. Windows are studied with the care a stage manager gives stage effects, designed and dressed in a studio before they go into the window. {{selfridge-roc}}

Make the first contact good. Before the public complete their first transactions they must come into direct contact with a member of staff, and on how that transaction is conducted depends largely the future goodwill or disrespect of the customer. {{selfridge-roc}}
Let staff learn from errors. The precept for staff is 'Don't make the same mistake twice.' {{selfridge-roc}}
Keep every statement dependable. Honesty always pays, and exaggerated statements of any kind are dangerous. {{selfridge-roc}}
Use figures. The sales manager must be an adept at figures, to whom a table of comparative percentages is as clear as the primer. {{selfridge-roc}}

blocks.x: Wikipedia describes a store that opened on 15 March 1909, with goods laid out for customers to examine and features that included a silence room. It credits him with promoting shopping for pleasure rather than necessity. {{selfridge}} {{selfridges}}

Selfridge sold in a large store with staff and a window budget. A small seller has a table, a phone and a few photographs. The thinking carries over as making the item easy to see and understand, and that adaptation is ours. {{selfridge-roc}}

Source
Your presentation

Greet and listen before you present
Don't make the same mistake twice
Keep a log of what went wrong and fix it

modules.name: Zig Ziglar
modules.outcome: Sort an objection into Ziglar's five reasons people do not buy, respond to the real one honestly, and check a price objection before answering it.
modules.intro: Zig Ziglar's Secrets of Closing the Sale is full of practical lists. We could not read the book, so this lesson uses a long summary, which reports his five reasons, his advice on price objections and on a no, and his line between a professional and a peddler.

blocks.x: The record behind this lesson

We read the first 100,000 characters of a book summary of the 1984 book, about three-quarters of it. It is secondary, and nothing here is a quotation from Ziglar. Check the book before you quote him. {{ziglar-sum}}
His method, step by step

i: Sort a no into its reason. The summary lists five: they feel they do not need what you sell; they do not have any money; they are in no rush; they do not want what you sell; they do not trust you. {{ziglar-sum}}

Treat many nos as requests for more. The summary says many people who say no are really saying 'tell me more', that you should not pressure them, and that you should give them new information so they can make a new decision. {{ziglar-sum}}
Check the price objection first. It says to repeat the objection as a question so the prospect has to defend it, and to verify that price is the real objection before responding. {{ziglar-sum}}
Do not argue. Objections thrive on opposition and die with agreement, so involve the prospect instead of lecturing. {{ziglar-sum}}

Know the named closes. Examples in the summary: the cost close (the price is paid once but the cost is maintenance over the product's life), the 1902 close (break the cost into a small figure), the 20/20 close (doing nothing about the problem costs more than acting) and the four questions close (like it, want it, can afford it, when to start). {{ziglar-sum}}

Keep the motive straight. Selling done for the prospect, not to the prospect, is professional, while recommending extras only to earn more makes you a peddler, and sincerity, trust and integrity are essential. {{ziglar-sum}}

blocks.x: We read a secondary summary, not the full book. Check the book before quoting. This module's lessons on objections, closing and fair selling still apply, and you should never pressure a buyer who has said no for a good reason. {{ziglar-sum}}

head: Reason in the summary
Question to find out
Honest response
rows: What would make this useful to you?
Return to their needs; accept if there is none
What would be comfortable for you?
Look at terms or a smaller option; say if it does not fit
Give true information about timing; do not invent a deadline
Offer an alternative or let them go
What would you need to know?
Slow down, give evidence, do what you say
blocks.src: The first column follows the summary. The other columns are our adaptation. {{ziglar-sum}}

blocks.x: Worked example: which of the five is it? (illustrative, our reading)

blocks.title: Sorting a price objection
steps: The buyer says: It is too expensive. First repeat it as a question: 'Too expensive compared with what?' {{ziglar-sum}}
Verify that price is the real objection. If they have no money, say so honestly and look at terms, a smaller option or a later date.
If they do not see the need, return to the questions that uncover needs.
If they do not trust you, slow down, give evidence and do what you say you will do.
Do not argue. Acknowledge the concern, then give information. {{ziglar-sum}}

blocks.x: Worked example: a cost close, honestly (invented numbers)

blocks.title: Total cost, not just price
steps: Product A costs £40 and lasts one year; product B costs £90 and lasts four years. Over four years A costs 4 × 40 = £160 and B costs £90.
Per year, A is £40 and B is £90 ÷ 4 = £22.50. The 1902 close would say B costs about £0.06 a day (22.50 ÷ 365). {{ziglar-sum}}
That is a fair comparison only if the lifetimes are true. State the evidence for the four years, or do not use the argument.
If B does not suit their need, say so, even if it costs you the sale.

modules.name: George Cadbury
modules.outcome: Write a personal code of fair dealing that covers your claims, your sources and what you do when you find a problem, using the Cadbury case with its delays and disputes.
modules.intro: George Cadbury's firm ran a model village and faced a hard test: cocoa it bought came from islands where labour was forced. The family's own account is detailed and sympathetic, and historians dispute the pace. The case shows fair dealing as a habit with costs.

blocks.x: The record behind this lesson

We read the Cadbury family trust's account of the campaign in full. It is adapted from a firm insider's history, so it is sympathetic, and the pace of the firm's action has been criticised. We also read a chapter on the firm's own organisation, including how it handled complaints, and Britannica, Wikipedia and two scholarly abstracts. {{wa-cadbury}} {{cadbury-1912}} {{brit-cadbury}} {{springer-cadbury}} {{jstor-higgs}}
His method, step by step

i: Start from a rumour and check it. In 1901 William Cadbury heard of forced labour on cocoa plantations in the islands of São Tomé and Príncipe, and then the firm received particulars of an estate for sale that listed 200 labourers among its assets. He wrote to anti-slavery campaigners, missionaries and other chocolate makers. {{wa-cadbury}}

Hope for the better case, and look anyway. The account says he hoped to find a situation less bad than the evidence suggested, but went on gathering evidence, including from a Scottish missionary, and visited Lisbon in March 1903. {{wa-cadbury}}

Weigh walking away. The account says it would have been easy to stop buying and wash their hands of it, but William wanted any injustice put right, and only about 5 per cent of São Tomé cocoa went to England, so withdrawal alone probably would not have helped. {{wa-cadbury}}

Get an independent investigator. In 1904 Cadbury, Fry, Rowntree and Stollwerck chose Joseph Burtt to investigate. He reported mortality of over 10 per cent of young adults even on the best estates, and on one plantation 80 deaths among 150 newcomers. {{wa-cadbury}}

Act, then wait on advice. The report went to the Foreign Office and to the Portuguese government in 1907. On the Foreign Office's advice William delayed publishing it and waited a further year for new rules to take effect. In October 1908 he and Burtt visited the islands and found the situation unchanged. {{wa-cadbury}}

Decide, and face the dispute. In March 1909 Cadbury Brothers announced it would make no further purchases of cocoa from the islands. In September 1908 the Standard had accused the firm of laggardliness, indifference and hypocrisy, and the firm sued for libel. {{wa-cadbury}}

blocks.x: The firm also had a standing way to look into complaints. Edward Cadbury's 1912 book says that when the Men's Works Committee began in 1905 its early work included the investigation of complaints received from customers, and that the organisation was designed so that no case of difficulty could arise without coming to the board's knowledge. That is the firm's own account. {{cadbury-1912}}

A scholarly chapter describes the firm spending a decade investigating, and an article on the episode describes it as an international scandal in which the firm was a major buyer. Critics argue that the delay mattered. {{springer-cadbury}} {{jstor-higgs}}

The main account of the investigation here is the family's own, which is sympathetic, and the pace of the firm's action has been criticised. We present the case to show how hard fair dealing can be, not as a clean success story. {{wa-cadbury}} {{jstor-higgs}}

steps: From the first rumour in 1901 to the announcement in March 1909 is 8 years, a little over 8 years. {{wa-cadbury}}
Burtt's 80 deaths among 150 newcomers is 80 ÷ 150 = 53%. {{wa-cadbury}}

A critic would ask whether the second year of waiting on the Foreign Office's advice cost lives. The account does not say, and we do not either. Fair dealing includes keeping a record of why you waited. {{jstor-higgs}}

I know where what I sell comes from, and I ask when I do not.

modules.name: Dale Carnegie
modules.outcome: Use Carnegie's principles on handling people to prepare and review your role-play, keep the interest sincere, and check yourself against his critics.
modules.intro: Dale Carnegie's principles on winning people to your way of thinking and on changing people without giving offence give a review checklist for a role-play. The book's critics supply the other half of the checklist.

blocks.x: The record behind this lesson
We did not read the book. The principles below are quoted as worded in the Wikipedia article's lists, and the criticism comes from the same article. {{carnegie-wiki}}
His method, step by step

i: Avoid the argument. The only way to get the best of an argument is to avoid it; show respect for the other person's opinions and never say 'You're wrong.' {{carnegie-wiki}}
Admit your own errors. If you're wrong, admit it quickly and emphatically; begin in a friendly way. {{carnegie-wiki}}
Let them talk. Let the other person do a great deal of the talking, and try honestly to see things from their point of view. {{carnegie-wiki}}
Give them the idea. Let the other person feel the idea is theirs; be sympathetic with their ideas and desires; appeal to the nobler motives. {{carnegie-wiki}}
Correct without giving offence. Begin with praise and honest appreciation; call attention to mistakes indirectly; talk about your own mistakes first; let the other person save face. {{carnegie-wiki}}

Check against the critics. Sinclair Lewis said the method taught people to pretend, and later scholars called Carnegie manipulative. A role-play review should ask, for each technique, whether it was sincere. {{carnegie-wiki}}

blocks.x: These principles can be used as tricks. 'Let the other person feel the idea is theirs' is a case where the line between helping and manipulating matters most. Use them with this module's fair-selling rules. {{carnegie-wiki}}

Source
Check in your review

blocks.x: Worked example: reviewing a role-play (invented numbers)

blocks.title: Talk share and checks
steps: A role-play lasts 12 minutes. You timed yourself speaking 7 minutes and the buyer 5 minutes.
Your share is 7 ÷ 12 = 58%, and the buyer's is 42%. A target such as 'buyer talks at least half' is our suggestion, not Carnegie's.
Next run: you speak 5 minutes and the buyer 7. The buyer's share is 7 ÷ 12 = 58%.
Mark each principle on the checklist as met, partly met or missed, and give one example from the recording for each.

blocks.x: Worked example: a sincerity check (illustrative)

blocks.title: The critics' question
steps: In the recording you said 'That's a great question' four times, and you meant it once.
A buyer may notice. Cut the phrase where it is not true, and replace it with a specific remark about the question.
Rewrite one line for each principle so it is true of this buyer, and keep only the lines that are.

i: Record a role-play with permission.
Time the talk share.
Mark each principle in the checklist with an example.
Mark every line you did not mean and rewrite it.
Write three things to keep and three to change, and run it again.

blocks.x: Record a role-play, mark it against the checklist and rewrite every line that was not sincere.

blocks.q: Which is a Carnegie principle for winning people to your way of thinking?
o: The only way to get the best of an argument is to avoid it
blocks.w: It is the first of the twelve ways to win people to your way of thinking. {{carnegie-wiki}}

blocks.q: What did the critics say the method risked?
blocks.w: Lewis and later scholars called it insincere and manipulative. {{carnegie-wiki}}

Admit your own errors and let people save face. {{carnegie-wiki}}
